newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank seeks to rein in dollar surge.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank seeks to rein in dollar surge.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday sought to brake the dollar's recent surge against the deutschemark, firmly stating that the U.S. currency's recovery from its 1995 lows had gone far enough, and said it was keeping a close eye on the ebullient German share market.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the German central bank, was "closely watching" developments on foreign exchange markets and was determined that the mark would remain strong in the run up to the euro launch in 1999.
"We are now in a phase in which the correction has clearly come to an end," Tietmeyer said of the dollar which had at its height clocked up gains of more than 14 percent against the mark this year.
"We will naturally watch the developments in markets. You can be sure that it is important for us that the mark remains a strong currency and enters the euro as a strong currency."
Tietmeyer was addressing a news conference after the Bundesbank's annual out-of-town council meeting, taking place this year in the picturesque Alpine town of Aschau, Bavaria.

His comments took almost a pfennig off the dollar's value in marks, which fell from 1.7620 marks to the dollar before the news conference to some 1.7540 immediately after. It eased to 1.7495 by 1240 GMT.
Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler reinforced Tietmeyer's commitment to a strong mark when he spoke with reporters after the meeting.

Asked about the dollar's appreciation against the mark this year, Zeitler said that the G7 meeting at the end of April had determined that the state of correction in the exchange rates had "more or less" come to an end.
"On the other hand, what we do not want is a push in the other direction," he said.
The Bundesbank also hinted at concern over asset price inflation.

Tietmeyer said the bank was watching developments on the German share market, which has experienced a boom that added 32 percent to the blue chip DAX index in the first half of 1997, partly fuelled by the dollar gains.

"I don't want to follow in the steps of (Alan) Greenspan," said Tietmeyer, referring to the U.S. Federal Reserve chairman whose warnings of "irrational exuberance" on markets in December sparked a rout on global stock markets.
"But the development on the German share market is certainly not evidence of a liquidity squeeze," he added.
The 30-share DAX, in a downward correction from repeated surges to new highs this week, ended Thursday's bourse trade down 63.48 points at 3,992.38. Its record high was 4,066.09.

Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said the DAX gains would be discussed at a review of developments in M3 money supply in two weeks' time. The central bank uses M3 as a key early inflation indicator when setting monetary policy.
But Tietmeyer said inflation essentially remained under control and there appeared little danger of a price jump.
He also said he did not expect the central bank to change its target corridor for M3 money supply developments.
The Bundesbank's 1997 target range is 3.5 to 6.5 percent.
M3 money supply grew in May at an annualised rate of 7.0 percent from the final quarter of 1996, just above the target. In April, M3 grew 6.7 percent.
The central bank left its interest rates unchanged at the meeting in line with economists' expectations. The discount rate remains at 2.50 percent and the Lombard at 4.50 percent.
The Bundesbank made no comment on the Bank of England's move to raise U.K. interest rates 1/4 point to 6.75 percent which took place shortly after the Bundesbank news conference.
But Tietmeyer noted that the exchange rate of the British pound was a reflection of the domestic situation there.

Commenting on the strength of sterling, Tietmeyer said that Britain was at a different stage in the economic cycle than Germany and was currently enjoying the fruits of structural reforms implemented in the past.

"I think the British pound very strongly reflects the domestic situation," he said. "But one must also look at the interest rate differential and at market expectations that the interest rate differential may change further."
